title: Opposition: one tempo between a win and a draw
outcomes: Takes the opposition in a king-and-pawn ending when it is the move that wins
Predicts win or draw for king and pawn against king, and sees that one tempo or one king square can flip it
Names three cases where 'the side not to move wins' fails: king level with the pawn, a king already on a key square, a rook pawn

steps.text: **King and pawn against a king** is often decided by one tempo. When the kings face each other with exactly one square between them, the side that has to move must give way. That is the **opposition**. Watch one pawn win in one position and only draw in a look-alike.

steps.caption: Black to move. Every Black move loses; one line is shown.

line.say: Black has to leave the facing square. Here the king goes to d7.
White's king moves forward to f6.

claims.statement: With Black to move, Black loses.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb:** the side that is *not* to move holds the opposition, and holding it wins. It is a heuristic with exceptions. You will meet three: a king that is only **level with** the pawn, a king already **two ranks in front** of the pawn, and a **rook pawn**. Predict each one first.

steps.title: Same pawn, the move changes
steps.prompt: Black to move wins for White. Change one thing: White to move. Does the result survive? Predict, then check.

steps.title: Same pawn, wrong king square
steps.prompt: Back to Black to move. Put White's king on d5 instead of e5. Is it still a win? Predict, then check.
Before each prediction: did you ask who was to move, or where each king stood? Which of the two did you check first, and which did you forget?
